title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together II
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting zeros from scratch for every wraparound window versus a fixed-size sliding window with modulo-wrapped indices.

sections.title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together II

content.title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together II

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a CIRCULAR binary array nums (the last element is considered adjacent to the first), return the minimum number of swaps required to group all the 1s present in the array together, in any single contiguous block, allowing that block to wrap around the end of the array.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The array is explicitly circular","A fixed-size sliding window whose indices must be taken modulo n, allowing wraparound"],["Otherwise identical to grouping 1s together in a straight line","The exact same \"minimize zeros in a fixed-size window\" reduction, just over a circular index space"]]}

blocks.text: This is the same reduction as the non-circular version: count k, the total number of 1s, and find the window of size k with the fewest zeros, that zero count is the minimum swaps needed. The only difference is that a window of size k is now allowed to wrap around from the end of the array back to the start.

blocks.title: Analogy: Grouping Beads Around a Circular Necklace
blocks.text: Picture beads of two colors threaded onto a circular necklace, rather than a straight strand. Grouping all the beads of one color together still means finding the best-positioned arc of a fixed length, except now that arc is allowed to pass through the point where the necklace loops back on itself.

blocks.caption: The array is circular: a window can wrap from the last index back to the first

blocks.text: There are 3 ones. Considering windows that may wrap around, the best one needs only 1 swap.
There are 3 ones. The wraparound window covering indices 4, 0, 1 is [1,1,1], already all ones, needing 0 swaps.
Edge case: the array is entirely 1s or entirely 0s
When there are no 1s, or every element is already 1, 0 swaps are needed, exactly as in the non-circular version.
Before treating this as a brand new problem, notice it is exactly the linear "group all 1s together" problem, with the array indices now wrapping using modulo arithmetic.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The reduction from before still applies exactly: the eventual grouped block has a fixed size, k, the total count of 1s, and the swaps needed for a candidate block equal its zero count.

Observation 2: The only change is which windows of size k are possible, a window may now start anywhere from index 0 to index n minus 1 and wrap around past index n minus 1 back to index 0.

Observation 3: Using index modulo n for every position inside a window automatically handles the wraparound without any special-casing.

Observation 4: The same sliding-window technique still applies, just with modulo arithmetic on the indices as the window slides.
This leads to the same fixed-size sliding window as the linear version, but with every index taken modulo n so the window can wrap around the end of the array.
Count the total ones k, then for every possible window start (0 through n minus 1), count the zeros in that window directly, using modulo n to wrap indices past the end.

items: Count k, the total number of 1s in nums.
For every starting index i from 0 to n minus 1, examine the k positions starting at i, wrapping each index modulo n.
Count the zeros in that window directly.
Track the minimum zero count seen across every starting position.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recount zeros from scratch for every window, wrapping with modulo n

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every window position is checked independently, with the modulo operation handling wraparound directly in the index calculation.
No memory is carried between different starting positions.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), recounting k elements for each of n possible window starts.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: just like the linear version, neighboring windows overlap almost entirely, and the wraparound handling does not change that redundancy.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recounting is still wasteful here: the circular structure does not change the fact that sliding the window by one position only swaps out one element for one new element.

What changes from the linear version: the "entering" and "leaving" indices must be computed with modulo n, so they correctly wrap past the end of the array.

The core idea: count the first window once, then slide n minus 1 more times, each time adjusting the zero count by exactly the entering and leaving elements, using modulo arithmetic for their positions.

Count the zeros in the window starting at index 0 directly. Then slide the window start forward n minus 1 more times; at each step, the index leaving the window is (start minus 1), and the index entering is (start plus k minus 1) taken modulo n. Adjust the zero count by those two elements and track the minimum.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: same sliding window as the linear version, indices wrapped with modulo n

blocks.text: The circular structure does not change how much a window differs from its neighbor, still exactly one leaving element and one entering element, it only changes how their positions are computed. Using modulo n for both the leaving and entering indices correctly reproduces every window, including those that wrap past the end of the array, while still adjusting the zero count in O(1) per step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass across all n possible window starts.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This problem is the linear "group all 1s together" problem with one added twist: indices wrap around using modulo n, allowing the grouped block to straddle the end of the array. The core sliding-window technique, and its O(1) per-step update, carries over unchanged.

items: Forgetting to use modulo n when computing the entering or leaving index, which would miss valid wraparound windows.
Treating this as a fundamentally different problem instead of recognizing it as the same reduction with circular indices.

blocks.text: Explicitly noting that this is the same reduction as the non-circular version, with only the index arithmetic changed to modulo n, shows the connection between the two problems has been recognized rather than solved from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how does the circular array change your approach", think: the same fixed-size window and swap-equals-zero-count reduction still apply, just with indices taken modulo n.

items: How would you adapt this solution if the array were doubly circular, or represented as a circular linked structure instead of an array?
Why does taking indices modulo n correctly reproduce every valid wraparound window without missing any?
Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together, the non-circular version of this exact problem.
Any circular-array sliding window problem, where modulo arithmetic on indices is the standard way to handle wraparound.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n times k) time; the optimized sliding window runs in O(n) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: the same fixed-size sliding window as the linear version, with indices wrapped using modulo n to allow the block to straddle the end of the array.
Core Idea: the minimum swap count for a candidate block still equals its zero count; only the definition of which windows are possible changes, to include wraparound ones.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized sliding window.
Most Important Observation: a circular array only changes how window indices are computed (modulo n), not the underlying reduction or technique.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the connection to the non-circular version is recognized; the modulo arithmetic is the only new detail.
One line memory trick: same window, same reduction, just wrap the indices with modulo n.
